456.title: If He took the ten
456.hook: what could the ungrateful say if the ten were taken too
456.howItsDone: Sikhs read this stanza in Sukhmani Sahib, and Sikh teaching treats gratitude to Waheguru as part of everyday remembrance rather than a separate ritual.

segments.voice: Yesterday, das basatoo: ten gifts put behind the back, and trust thrown away over the one. Your line was ten given, one held back. Today the same stanza asks a sharp question.

Back to the birthday table. The child is still sulking over the eleventh present. Now take the whole table away. Not ten and a missing one: nothing. No cake, no wrapping paper, no party. What would there be to complain about then? Who would there be to complain to? It's a question that stops a sulk in its tracks, and it isn't asked to frighten anyone. It's asked to turn the head around. Guru Arjan asks it in the very next line, and then, surprisingly, he doesn't leave anyone at the empty table.
screen: `NOW THE TABLE IS EMPTY.` → `WHO WOULD YOU COMPLAIN TO?` → `A QUESTION THAT TURNS THE HEAD.`

segments.voice: The line goes: ek bhee na dei, das bhee hir lei. If He gave not even the one, and took back the ten as well. Then: tau moorhaa kahu kahaa karei. Then tell me, what could the fool do? Moorhaa is a blunt word: the foolish one, the one not thinking. The answer is in the silence after the question. Nothing. No court to appeal to, no account to draw on. Everything on the table came from the same hands. So the stanza goes on: jis thaakur sio naahee chaaraa. With the Master before whom we have no leverage, no say. Taa kau keejai sad namaskaaraa: to Him, bow, always. That could sound like fear: bow, because you have no choice. But the next line changes the whole stanza. Jaa kai man laagaa prabh meethaa: in whose mind God has come to taste sweet. Sarab sookh taahoo man voothaa: every comfort comes to live in that mind. Meethaa is sweet, the taste of sugar on the tongue. So the sum turns into something else. The person who sees the ten and thanks for them isn't cornered into bowing. They've started to love the Giver, and gratitude stops being a duty and becomes a taste. From the empty table, to the full one, to the hands that set it.
screen: `IF HE TOOK THE TEN AS WELL.` · `WHAT COULD THE FOOL DO?` · `BOW TO THE MASTER, ALWAYS.` · `MEETHAA: GOD TASTES SWEET.` · then, large: `THANK FOR THE TEN.`

segments.voice: Pick one tiny thing, the warmth of a cup in your hand, a sock without a hole, light from one window, and notice it as if it had been taken away and handed back. If you pray, thank the Giver for it in your own way; if not, just let yourself be glad of it, slowly, the way something sweet sits on your tongue.
Meethaa, sweet. Ek bhee na dei, das bhee hir lei: if not even one were given, and the ten taken too, what could anyone do?
Your line: thank for the ten. The empty table asks; the full one answers. Day four hundred fifty-six, done.

457.title: Living ashtpadi 5
457.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of all they have as Waheguru's gift held in trust, and gratitude is part of daily remembrance, including in the Ardas, which gives thanks before it asks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, meethaa: the empty table, and the mind where God tastes sweet. Your line was thank for the ten. Today, ashtpadi five lived, with one more picture from it.

A moneylender, a saahu, hands a trader capital to work with. The trader buys, sells, eats well, throws a wedding. Years pass, and he starts to think of the money as his own. Then one day the saahu asks for some of it back. Not all. Some. And the trader is furious, as though he's being robbed. Anyone watching can see what's happened, anyone except the trader. The second stanza of ashtpadi five tells a story like that, and it shows what gratitude is for.
screen: `THE SAAHU LENDS HIS CAPITAL.` → `YEARS PASS; IT FEELS LIKE MINE.` → `ASKED FOR SOME, HE'S FURIOUS.`

segments.voice: Guru Arjan tells it plainly. The banker gives his capital. The man eats and drinks and lives in delight. Then the banker takes back a little of what was only ever held in trust, and the ignorant one rages. By his anger he loses his own credit; nobody will trust him with anything again. Then the turn: the wise one places what belongs to the owner back before the owner, and accepts the order with his forehead bowed. That person, the stanza says, is made happy four times over. Put that next to the last three days. The salok named God the Giver. The ten things showed how gifts slip behind our backs. The empty table asked what anyone could say if they were all gone. Now the banker shows the long game. Gratitude isn't only a nice feeling. It's how you stay trustworthy with what you've been lent. The trader who forgot it was a loan couldn't let any of it go. And everything goes, in the end: health, strength, time, people you love. Sikh teaching doesn't pretend otherwise. What it offers is a way of holding it all now, as a trust, so that when some is called back, the hands are already open. That's why gratitude is this ashtpadi's practice: not a mood, but a habit of counting, so the ten never fall behind the back.

segments.voice: Name ten gifts you'd feel the loss of, someone's voice, your hands, a friend who still calls, a place that feels like home, and after each one, quietly add the word: lent. Not to make you sad, only to see them as the stanza does; then close your eyes and breathe with all ten held lightly.
Saahu, a banker or moneylender: ashtpadi five's practice is gratitude, seeing what we have as the banker's capital, lent and not owned.
Your line: count the ten. A loan, held with open hands. Four hundred fifty-seven, and counting.

458.title: Ashtpadi 6, salok: the thieves leave
458.hook: lust, anger, greed and attachment go, and pride too, by grace
458.howItsDone: Sikhs name kaam, krodh, lobh, moh and ahankaar as the five thieves, and in this salok of Sukhmani Sahib the request is for the Guru's grace against them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saahu: the banker's capital, held in trust. Your line was count the ten. Today, ashtpadi six begins.

You may remember them from last year: the five thieves. Kaam, lust. Krodh, anger. Lobh, greed. Moh, attachment. Ahankaar, pride. Elsewhere the Guru Granth Sahib pictures five thieves living inside the body, quietly carrying off whatever is valuable. Last year they came as a list. Ashtpadi six opens by naming them again, all five, in a single line. But this time the salok isn't describing the thieves. It's asking for something, and what it asks for is the surprise.
screen: `THE FIVE THIEVES, AGAIN.` → `LIVING IN THE HOUSE OF THE BODY.` → `THIS TIME, THE SALOK ASKS.`

segments.voice: The salok's first line lists them: kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, and then ahanmev, pride, the sense of I alone, I myself. And it asks that they be destroyed, that they go. You might expect the second line to give a method: five steps, a discipline for each thief. Instead it says: Nanak has come to God's sanctuary; bless me with Your grace, O divine Guru. The word for sanctuary is saranaagatee, coming for refuge, the way someone being chased runs to a protected house. The word for grace is prasaad, a gift freely given. So the salok's answer to the five thieves isn't a fight in the dark. It's a door, and a request: run to the safe house, and ask. That doesn't mean Sikhs sit back and do nothing. Elsewhere the Gurus speak of effort and of an honest, disciplined life. But this salok says something about where the change finally comes from. Pride can't be beaten by more pride, even pride in being humble. Anger can't be shouted down. The house is cleared by grace, coming in from outside. And that sets up all of ashtpadi six. Over the next days it repeats one phrase again and again: jih prasaad, by whose grace.
screen: `LUST, ANGER, GREED, ATTACHMENT, PRIDE.` · `SARANAAGATEE: RUN FOR REFUGE.` · `PRASAAD: A GIFT FREELY GIVEN.` · `CLEARED FROM OUTSIDE, NOT FOUGHT.` · then, large: `GRACE CLEARS THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Without judging yourself, let one of the five come to mind, the one you know best, lust, anger, greed, clinging or pride, and just name it. Breathe in slowly, as if the door of the house were opening, and as you breathe out, picture that thief walking out through it; you're not chasing it, only making room, and if you pray, ask for grace in your own way.
Saranaagatee, coming for refuge: ashtpadi six's salok names the five thieves, and asks for grace, prasaad, from the sanctuary of the Guru.
Your line: grace clears the house. Five thieves, and one open door to the sanctuary. Until tomorrow.

459.title: By whose grace
459.hook: jih prasaad: by whose grace you eat fine foods and wear fine clothes, remember Him
459.howItsDone: Many Sikhs remember Waheguru before eating, and in the gurdwara karah prashad is received in cupped hands as a gift of grace; ashtpadi six's 'jih prasaad' refrain is read as part of Sukhmani Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saranaagatee: five thieves, and a request for grace from the Guru's sanctuary. Your line was grace clears the house. Today, that word grace becomes a drumbeat.

Jih prasaad. Jih prasaad. Jih prasaad. Read ashtpadi six aloud and those two words come round again and again, at the start of line after line, like a drum keeping time under a song. By whose grace. Each time, a different gift follows, and the gifts in the first stanza are surprisingly ordinary for a sacred text. Not visions. Not miracles. Dinner. Perfume. A comfortable house. A good shirt. Things used every day without a second thought.
screen: `JIH PRASAAD, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `A DRUM UNDER THE SONG.` → `DINNER, PERFUME, A GOOD SHIRT.`

segments.voice: Jih means by whom, by whose. Prasaad, you met yesterday: grace, a gift freely given. In the gurdwara, the sweet offering given into cupped hands at the end of a service is called karah prashad, and today's word can be heard in its name. So jih prasaad: by whose free gift. The first stanza goes like this. By whose grace you eat the thirty-six delicacies, a phrase read as every kind of fine food, keep that Master in your mind. By whose grace you put fragrance on your body, remembering Him you reach the highest state. By whose grace you live in a house of comfort, meditate on Him always. And the next stanza picks up the clothes: by whose grace you wear silks and fine cloth, why abandon Him and cling to another? Every line has two halves. First, a gift you can taste, smell or touch. Then a turning: remember, keep in mind, don't forget. Guru Arjan doesn't ask anyone to give up the meal or the shirt. He asks for the meal to become a reminder. It's the same move as the ten things, made smaller and more frequent: not once a year at a feast, but every time you sit down to eat.
screen: `JIH: BY WHOSE. PRASAAD: FREE GIFT.` · `THE THIRTY-SIX DELICACIES.` · `EACH GIFT, THEN A TURNING.` · `THE MEAL BECOMES A REMINDER.` · then, large: `BY HIS GRACE, THIS MEAL.`

segments.voice: Picture the next thing you'll eat, a plate, a sandwich, a cup of tea, and see where it came from: a field, a farmer, a truck, a shop, someone's hands. Then let the drumbeat come: jih prasaad, by whose grace. If you pray, let that be your thanks; if you don't, let it be a moment of noticing that none of it began with you.
Jih prasaad. By whose grace: the refrain of ashtpadi six, set before every ordinary gift.
Your line: by his grace, this meal. Grace, set at the table. Day four hundred fifty-nine, done.

460.title: By whose grace, the body
460.hook: by His grace you have a healthy body and a home
460.howItsDone: Sikhs read the 'jih prasaad' stanzas of Sukhmani Sahib as reminders that health, home and family are gifts, and many share what they have through langar and seva.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jih prasaad: the drumbeat over dinner and a good shirt. Your line was by his grace, this meal. Today the same two words come closer to home.

Most of us only notice our bodies when something goes wrong. A sprained ankle, and every step is a project. A cold, and you'd give anything for one clear breath through the nose. Then it heals, and within a week you've forgotten again. The same with home: you notice the roof the night it leaks. Ashtpadi six keeps saying jih prasaad, by whose grace, and in its later stanzas it turns to the two things we forget most completely: the body we live in, and the house that holds it.
screen: `NOTICED ONLY WHEN IT HURTS.` → `THE ROOF, THE NIGHT IT LEAKS.` → `BY WHOSE GRACE: BODY AND HOME.`

segments.voice: One line says: jih prasaad aarog kanchan dehee. By whose grace you have a healthy, golden body. Aarog is health, being free of illness. Kanchan is gold. Dehee is the body. A golden body isn't about looks: in the old poetry, gold is what's precious and doesn't tarnish. The second half, as always, turns: attune yourself to that loving Lord. The same ashtpadi has already spoken of the house: by whose grace you live in a mansion of comfort, by whose grace you dwell at peace with your family. Another line says, by whose grace your honor is kept covered: the things you'd rather nobody saw, quietly protected. Put those together and you get an ordinary good day. You woke up, you could move, nobody embarrassed you, there was a door to close behind you and people inside it. The stanza says none of that is automatic. Each is a jih prasaad. This doesn't mean anyone who is ill, or without a home, has lost grace. Gurbani speaks of rich and poor, healthy and sick, as living within the same hukam, and Sikhs are asked to share what they have, which is why the langar, the gurdwara kitchen, serves a free meal to anyone who comes in. The stanza speaks to the one who has these things and forgets them, and asks that person to notice.

segments.voice: Start at your feet, which carried you today, then your hands, which held things, then your lungs, breathing all by themselves; whatever hurts, let it be there too, you're not pretending. Then widen out to the room, the walls, the roof, whoever shares this home with you, or the quiet if no one does. If you pray, give thanks with the words jih prasaad; if you don't, let each part simply be noticed and valued.
Dehee, the body. By whose grace a healthy, precious body, and a home to live in.
Your line: by his grace, this home. A roof, a door, and people inside it. See you tomorrow.

461.title: Living ashtpadi 6
461.hook: every comfort points back to a Giver
461.howItsDone: In everyday Punjabi speech Sikhs often credit good news to 'Waheguru di kirpa', Waheguru's grace, while also thanking the people involved; ashtpadi six gives that habit its scripture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dehee: a healthy body, a house, honor kept covered. Your line was by his grace, this home. Today, ashtpadi six, lived.

A grandmother is asked how she is, and before any news comes a small phrase: Waheguru di kirpa naal. By Waheguru's grace. The harvest was good, by grace. The grandson passed his exams, by grace. The knee is better, by grace. It can sound like a habit of speech, and partly it is. But habits of speech are where a teaching goes to live. Sukhmani's sixth ashtpadi says jih prasaad, by whose grace, line after line. In homes like hers, the refrain kept going long after the reading ended.
screen: `HOW ARE YOU? BY GRACE.` → `A HABIT OF SPEECH.` → `WHERE A TEACHING GOES TO LIVE.`

segments.voice: Kirpaa is another word for grace, kindness, favor. In ashtpadi four you met it in the child's prayer: in Your kirpaa are countless comforts. Ashtpadi six spreads the same thought across a whole life: food, scent, clothes, house, family, health, honor. Every comfort, a gift. What does living that look like? Take one comfort, a hot cup of tea, and trace it back. Someone boiled the water, maybe you. The water came through pipes someone laid, from rain that fell on hills you'll never see. The leaves were picked by hands, maybe in Assam or Kenya or Sri Lanka, by people who got up before dawn. The milk came from an animal someone cared for. The warmth came from fire, or a power line, or the sun. Go back far enough and every comfort runs out of human causes and arrives at something none of us made. That's where Sikh teaching places the Giver: not instead of the farmer and the plumber, but behind and through all of them. So living ashtpadi six means two things at once: real thanks to the people, by name if you can, and beneath that, jih prasaad, by whose grace any of it exists at all. The grandmother's phrase holds both. The harvest was good because people worked. And by grace.
screen: `KIRPAA: GRACE, KINDNESS, FAVOR.` · `ONE CUP OF TEA, TRACED BACK.` · `PAST THE PEOPLE, TO THE GIVER.` · `THANKS TO BOTH, AT ONCE.` · then, large: `EVERY COMFORT A GIFT.`

segments.voice: Choose something you're touching right now, the chair, your clothes, the light, and ask where it came from, then where that came from, naming the people you pass on the way, even only as the ones who made it and the ones who carried it. Keep going until you run out of people, and rest there, at the edge of what anyone made. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, or simply sit there grateful.
Kirpaa, grace, kindness, favor. Every comfort points back, through many hands, to a Giver: jih prasaad, by whose grace.
Your line: every comfort a gift. Thanks for the people, and past them, for the Giver. That's day four hundred sixty-one.

462.title: Ashtpadi 7, salok: the holy company
462.hook: the salok praises the company of the holy
462.howItsDone: Sikhs gather as sangat, the congregation, in the gurdwara to sing and hear the Guru's word and to eat together in langar; ashtpadi seven of Sukhmani Sahib praises that holy company.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirpaa: one cup of tea, traced back past every hand to the Giver. Your line was every comfort a gift. Today, a new stretch of Sukhmani begins, ashtpadis seven to twelve.

Some people walk into a room and make it a little easier to be good. Nobody feels judged around them. Conversations get kinder; the complaining slows; the laughter gets more honest. People leave having been a better version of themselves for an hour, without trying. For several ashtpadis, Sukhmani has talked about the Giver and the gifts. Now, in the seventh, it turns to people: the holy, and what happens to us in their company.
screen: `SOMEONE WHO MAKES GOOD EASIER.` → `NOT JUDGED, JUST BETTER.` → `NOW SUKHMANI TURNS TO PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: The salok has four short lines. First: the Supreme Lord is agam, out of reach, and agaadh, too deep to sound. Second: whoever speaks of Him is set free. Third: listen, friend, Nanak prays. And fourth: saadh janaa kee acharaj kathaa. The story of the holy ones is wondrous. Saadh, or saadhoo, is a holy person, someone whose life has been shaped by the Name. Acharaj is wonder, the feeling of seeing something you didn't think was possible. Notice the order. The salok starts with God beyond reach, and ends with people you can actually sit beside. That's the bridge this ashtpadi builds: the One too deep to sound becomes nearer in the company of those who remember Him. In Sikh life that has a concrete shape: the sangat, the congregation, singing together in the gurdwara and eating side by side in the langar. Over the next days, the ashtpadi lists what happens in that company. And this is where the week ends. Six days ago, if He took the ten, and the mind where God tastes sweet. The banker's capital, lent, not owned. The five thieves and grace that clears the house. Jih prasaad over dinner, the body and the home. Every comfort a gift. A week of the Giver. Now, the Giver's people.
screen: `AGAM, AGAADH: BEYOND REACH.` · `LISTEN, FRIEND, NANAK PRAYS.` · `ACHARAJ: THE WONDROUS STORY.` · `GOD FAR, THE HOLY NEAR.` · then, large: `GOOD COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person in whose presence you become a little better, a grandparent, a teacher, a friend, someone you sat beside once and never forgot, and remember one thing they said, or the way they listened. Notice what your body does as you remember them; maybe the shoulders soften, maybe the jaw unclenches. If you pray, give thanks for them, and breathe out whatever you don't need to carry.
Acharaj, wonder. The salok calls God beyond reach, and the story of the holy ones wondrous.
Your line: good company. Some people make good a little easier, just by being there. A week, done.
